questions.q: Why does pinned (page-locked) memory transfer to the GPU faster than ordinary pageable memory?
options: Pinned memory uses a smaller data type automatically
Pinned memory stays at a fixed physical address, so the GPU's DMA engine can transfer it directly instead of going through an extra staging copy
Pinned memory is stored on the GPU itself
Pinned memory compresses the data before transfer
questions.explain: Because pinned memory can't be moved or swapped by the OS, the DMA engine can read it directly, skipping the intermediate staging buffer pageable memory requires.

questions.q: How do you make a PyTorch `DataLoader` produce batches in pinned memory?
options: Set `num_workers=0`
Pass `pin_memory=True` to the `DataLoader` constructor
Call `.cuda()` on the dataset
Set `batch_size=1`
questions.explain: `DataLoader(..., pin_memory=True)` allocates each produced batch tensor in page-locked memory before it reaches the training loop.

questions.q: What happens if you call `.to(device, non_blocking=True)` on a tensor from ordinary (unpinned) memory?
options: It raises a RuntimeError immediately
The transfer silently happens synchronously anyway, since the driver must stage unpinned memory through a pinned buffer first
It automatically pins the memory for you with no cost
It transfers at double speed
questions.explain: `non_blocking=True` only produces an actual asynchronous transfer when the source memory is already pinned; otherwise the copy happens synchronously regardless of the flag.

questions.q: What is the main performance benefit of combining `pin_memory=True` with `non_blocking=True`?
options: It reduces the model's parameter count
It allows the next batch's transfer to overlap with the GPU's compute on the current batch, instead of happening in series
It eliminates the need for a GPU entirely
It automatically increases batch size
questions.explain: Asynchronous, pinned transfers let data movement for the next batch hide behind the current batch's compute, which can keep the GPU from starving each iteration.

questions.q: Why isn't it recommended to pin every tensor in a program indiscriminately?
options: Pinning is a system call that locks physical pages, and over-pinning can starve the rest of the system's memory
Pinned tensors cannot be used in any GPU computation
PyTorch limits programs to one pinned tensor at a time
Pinning permanently disables `non_blocking` transfers
questions.explain: Pinning memory has a real system cost — it locks physical pages so the OS can't reclaim them — so it's used selectively for data that benefits, like dataloader batches.
